🧰 Use AI well · Step 4 of 4 · 5 min

Keep yourself safe

What never to type, fakes that look real, and who answers for the result.

🔒 What you type leaves your device

Most chatbots do not work inside your phone or computer. When you press “Send”, your message travels over the internet to the computers of the company that owns the chatbot.

There it is usually stored. People who work for the company may read some messages, and your chats may become examples that later AI models learn from. How much of this happens depends on the service and on its settings.

So treat a chat like a postcard, not like a diary. A postcard has no envelope, so other people can read it too. Type only what you would let a stranger read.

Task. Is it safe to send this to a chatbot, or should you never send it?

Show the solution

A question, a textbook problem and your own poem have nothing private in them. A password, an address, a document or a bank card can cause real trouble if a stranger gets it. A friend's secret is not yours, so do not share it. If you have already sent something like this, tell an adult you trust, and change the password.

Task. Which of these is safe to send to a chatbot?

Show the answer

Right answer: A paragraph of your own essay about rivers

What you send to a chatbot is usually stored on a company's computers, and people who work there may read some of it. An essay about rivers has nothing private in it. A password, your name with your address, and a friend's private messages must stay out of a chat.

🎭 Seeing is no longer proof

AI can make a photo, a video or a voice recording of something that never happened. For example, a real person “says” words they never said. A fake like this is called a deepfake. A short recording can be enough to copy a voice.

Some fakes have mistakes you can see: strange hands, letters that make no sense, a blurry edge around a face. But a good fake may have none. So check the source, not the pixels: where it comes from, not how it looks. Ask yourself two questions:

1. Who published this?
2. Do trusted news sources report it too?

Not sure which news sources can be trusted? Ask an adult you trust: a parent or a teacher.

Task. You see a shocking video of a famous person saying something terrible. What is the best first step?

Show the answer

Right answer: Before you believe or share it, check whether trusted news sources report it

AI can fake a video of a real person, and a good fake can look normal. If a famous person really said this, trusted news sources would very likely report it. Until you have checked, do not share it.

📞 The trick with a familiar voice

A scammer is a person who tricks others to get their money. With a copied voice, a scammer can call you or send a voice message. It sounds like someone from your family: “I am in trouble. Send money now, and tell nobody.”

Hurry, secrecy and money together are a stop sign. Send nothing. Hang up and call that family member yourself, on the number you already know. Then tell an adult you trust.

Some families agree on a secret code word for calls like this: a word that only the family knows.

Task. A voice message that sounds like your brother says: “I am in trouble. Send money right now and tell nobody.” What is the best thing to do?

Show the answer

Right answer: Call him on the number you know, and tell an adult

A voice can be copied, and a scammer who is asked “Is this really you?” will simply answer “yes”. Waiting checks nothing, and if your brother really is in trouble, it does not help him. Calling back works because you choose the number, so you reach your real brother. And an adult can help you decide what to do next.

⚖️ AI can be unfair

An AI model learns from examples made by people. If the examples are one-sided or unfair, the model can learn that too: it may work worse for some groups of people, or prefer some people over others. This is called bias.

A real case: a program for choosing workers was trained on the job applications that one company had received over ten years. Most came from men, so the program began to rate women's applications lower. The company stopped the project.

So when AI helps to decide something about a person (a grade, a job, a loan), it is fair to ask why, and to ask a human to look at the decision again.

Think first. A chatbot gives you an answer, and you use it. Who is responsible for what happens next?

Show the answer

You are. A chatbot does not decide to hand in your homework, send your message or sign your name. You do.

The company that built a chatbot is responsible for how it works. But if you publish, send or hand in something, you are responsible for it, wherever the words came from.

“The chatbot said so” does not undo a mistake. That is why checking is your job, not the chatbot's.

Task. Match each risk with the habit that protects you.

Show the solution

A chatbot can make a fact up, so a second source has to confirm it. A fake video can look perfect, so you check where it comes from. A voice can be copied, so you call back yourself, on a number you know. And what you never typed, nobody can read.

Task. A chatbot is friendly, always there and never tired. Which statement about it is true?

Show the answer

Right answer: It is a program that guesses the next words: it sounds kind, but it is not a person

A chatbot can be useful, and talking to it can even feel good. But its kind words are text written by a program: it is not a person, your chats are not secret, and it can be wrong. If something hurts or frightens you, tell a person you trust: a parent, a teacher, a friend.

Remember

  • A chat is a postcard, not a diary: no passwords, addresses, documents or other people's secrets.
  • A photo, a voice or a video is not proof: AI can fake them, and such a fake is called a deepfake. Check who published it and whether trusted news sources report it.
  • Hurry, secrecy and money together are a stop sign: hang up and call back on a number you know.
  • You are responsible for what you do with an AI answer, so checking is your job. AI can be wrong, and it can be unfair (this is called bias).
